title: Layer-by-layer Collagen Deposition in Microfluidic Devices for Microtissue Stabilization
protocol: Prepare or purchase 200 mg of acidified, soluble type I collagen from rat tails.
Dilute 100 mg of native, acidified collagen solution to a concentration of 0.5 mg/ml with ice cold sterile water.
Adjust the pH of the diluted collagen solution to 9–10 using a few drops of 1 N NaOH and stir at room temperature for 30 min.
Centrifuge the precipitated collagen solution at 3,000 × g for 25 min.
Aspirate and dispose of the supernatant fluid from the centrifuged solution.
Resuspend the precipitated collagen in 200 ml of methanol with 0.1 N HCl.
Allow the methylation reaction to occur by stirring at room temperature for 4 days.
Centrifuge the solution at 3,000 × g for 25 min after the methylation period.
Aspirate and dispose of the acidified methanol supernatant.
Dissolve methylated collagen in 25 ml of sterile PBS to achieve a concentration of approximately 3 mg/ml.
Pipette the solution repeatedly to ensure thorough mixing.
Filter the solution through a 60 μm cell strainer.
Adjust the pH of the solution to 7.3–7.4 using increments of 1 N NaOH.
Assess the concentration of the solution using a commercial rat collagen ELISA kit or hydroxyproline assay kit.
Dilute the solution to 3 mg/ml with sterile PBS if necessary.
Sterilize the methylated collagen solution by transferring it to a glass bottle, carefully layering 3 ml of chloroform at the bottom, and storing overnight at 4 °C.
Aseptically remove and store the top layer, which is the sterilized methylated collagen.
Store the sterilized solution at 4 °C for use within 1 month.
Dilute 100 mg of native, acidified (pH 2–3) collagen to a concentration of 0.5 mg/ml with ice-cold sterile water and keep on ice.
Adjust the pH of the collagen solution to 9–10 using drops of 1 N NaOH.
Stir the solution at room temperature for 30 min.
The collagen should precipitate, causing the solution to become cloudy.
Dissolve 40 mg of succinic anhydride in 10 ml of acetone.
Slowly add the succinic anhydride-acetone mixture to the collagen solution in approximately 0.5 ml increments while stirring.
Maintain the pH above 9.0 by adding drops of 1 N NaOH as needed.
Continue stirring at room temperature for 120 minutes after all succinic anhydride is added.
Periodically check and maintain the pH above 9.0.
Adjust the pH to 4.0 with increments of 1 N HCl, observing the solution becoming cloudy again.
Centrifuge the solution at 3,000 × g for 25 minutes to pellet the succinylated collagen.
Aspirate and dispose of the acidified supernatant containing unreacted succinic anhydride.
Dissolve the pelleted succinylated collagen in 25 ml of sterile PBS using repeated pipetting.
Filter the solution through a 60 µm cell strainer.
Adjust the pH to 7.3–7.4 using increments of 1 N NaOH.
Assess the concentration of the succinylated collagen solution.
Dilute the solution to 3 mg/ml with sterile PBS if necessary.
Sterilize the succinylated collagen solution by transferring it to a glass bottle with a screw cap.
Layer 3 ml of chloroform at the bottom of the bottle.
Set the bottle O/N at 4 °C.
Aseptically remove and store the top layer as the succinylated collagen.
Store the succinylated collagen solution at 4 °C for use within 1 month.
Prepare 1 ml samples from each of the native, methylated, and succinylated collagen solutions.
Dilute the samples to a concentration of 0.1 mg/ml with sterile pure water.
Perform hydrogen ion titration on each sample as described by Tanford.
Adjust the pH of the solutions to 7.3 with small amounts of NaOH and HCl.
Plot the change in pH per volume of acid added versus the number of bound H+ ions per molecule.
Dialyze the buffer at least 1,000-fold against water through a 10 kDa cutoff membrane using 3 solution changes for at least 4 hr each.
Assess the efficacy of the succinylation reaction using the TNBA colorimetric method.
Fabricate microfluidic devices using standard methods.
Create microfluidic cell culture chambers with 100 µm tall, 0.4–1.5 mm wide, and 1–10 mm long channels for cell growth.
Oxidize the surfaces of the device and a glass slide using a plasma cleaner.
Press together the oxidized surfaces to bond the microfluidic device.
Sterilize the device by exposure to UV light for at least 30 min.
Fill the chamber with 50 µg/ml fibronectin in sterile PBS.
Incubate the filled chamber at 37 °C for 45 min.
Seed the device with primary rat or human hepatocytes.
Allow the cells to attach for 4–6 hr.
Wash out unattached cells.
Replace the plating media with growth media.
Incubate overnight to ensure full cell spreading and create a confluent monolayer of cells.
In a laminar flow tissue culture hood, prepare sufficient volumes of methylated and succinylated collagen solutions for 10 applications per device.
Keep the prepared collagen solutions on ice.

Begin with the methylated (polycationic) collagen solution and alternate flushing the devices with 20 μl of methylated and then succinylated collagen solutions, waiting 1 min between each application.
Flush the device a total of 10 times per solution to complete one round for both methylated and succinylated collagen applications.
Observe collagen accumulation at the inlet/outlet depending on its size during layering.
If resistance to fluid flow increases, flush the device once or twice with media before continuing.
After applying all layers, rinse the device twice with fresh media and return it to the incubator.
Prepare representative devices for transmission electron microscopy using standard methods to verify collagen matrix assembly.
Image the cell morphology using phase contrast microscopy.
For viability assessment, perform LIVE/DEAD staining according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Incubate the stained cells for 30 min at 37 °C.
Rinse the device with PBS after incubation.
Image the device using fluorescence microscopy.
For apical polarization analysis, prepare CMFDA dye solution with DAPI as instructed by the manufacturer.
Incubate the cells with CMFDA staining solution for 30 min at 37 °C.
Rinse the device again with PBS.
Image the device using fluorescence microscopy.
Collect spent media at appropriate time points during culture duration.
Measure albumin and urea levels in the collected media to assess cell function.
Perform endpoint functional analyses on the cells themselves.
Assess enzyme activity levels.
Conduct antibody staining.
Carry out RNA analysis.
Induce cytochrome P450 enzyme activities in hepatocytes.
Measure phase II conjugation enzyme glutathione S-transferase activities in hepatocytes.
